texts.0: SP, due to joining the initial straight off the navigation route without levelling at the briefed pattern altitude, arrived at the break point with an uncontrolled vertical trend. Break altitude deviated beyond 300 feet and the trend continued through the roll. The IP intervened on the controls to reposition the aircraft in the break zone at the correct altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power reduction during the recovery to the field, allowed the aircraft to leave the briefed pattern altitude before the break point. Break altitude reached the 300 feet limit and was corrected only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP. The briefed altitude was regained late, well into the turn to downwind.
texts.2: SP, due to changing pitch attitude before the power was set on the initial, allowed break altitude to leave the 150 feet band. The deviation reached approximately 250 feet before SP identified it on the altimeter and re-established the briefed altitude unaided. The correction was complete before roll-out on downwind.
texts.3: SP levelled off from the navigation recovery and flew the break at the briefed pattern altitude, with deviations held inside 150 feet through the roll and the deceleration. Power and pitch were set before the break point, so no vertical excursion developed. Altitude control required no prompting at any stage.
texts.4: SP arrived at the initial already stabilized and completed the break with altitude deviations barely readable on the altimeter. Pitch, power and trim were set ahead of the break point, so the roll was flown with no correction required at all.
texts.marginal: SP held break altitude within the required standard, but the deviations sat near the outer edge of the 150 feet band on each pattern and always in the climbing sense. The tendency is to let the nose rise as bank is applied at the break point. SP is expected to complete the level-off and trim the aircraft earlier on the initial so that altitude is captured before the break.

texts.0: SP, due to an aggressive roll input made without reference to the attitude indicator, exceeded the briefed break bank by more than 15 degrees. The excessive bank was not reduced as the turn progressed and produced downwind spacing that could not be recovered. The IP took control to unload the aircraft and re-establish the briefed bank.
texts.1: SP, due to an unmonitored roll rate at the break point, applied a bank that reached the 15 degrees deviation limit from the briefed value. The bank was reduced only after the IP called the attitude, and the correct value was re-established late in the turn. Downwind spacing had to be adjusted as a result.
texts.2: SP, due to a roll input applied faster than briefed, allowed break bank to deviate past the 10 degrees band. The deviation reached approximately 13 degrees before SP cross-checked the attitude indicator and set the briefed bank without assistance. Downwind spacing was unaffected.
texts.3: SP established the briefed break bank promptly and held it within 10 degrees throughout the turn. The roll rate was smooth and the bank was cross-checked against the attitude indicator, producing the planned downwind spacing.
texts.4: SP set the briefed break bank in a single smooth input and held it with deviations not measurable on the attitude indicator. The resulting downwind spacing matched the briefed value with no adjustment.
texts.marginal: SP kept break bank within the required standard, but the values sat consistently at the shallow edge of the 10 degrees band. The tendency is to under-bank at the break and then add a second correcting input. SP is expected to establish the briefed bank in one deliberate roll and confirm it on the attitude indicator.

texts.0: SP, due to trimming the aircraft only after the gear and flaps were selected, allowed downwind altitude to deviate beyond 300 feet from the briefed pattern altitude. The deviation persisted to the abeam position without being recognized. The IP intervened on the controls to re-establish the pattern altitude before the turn to base.
texts.1: SP, due to attention held on the configuration changes instead of the altimeter, let downwind altitude reach the 300 feet deviation limit. The altitude was corrected only after the IP prompted twice, and the pattern altitude was regained just before the turn to base.
texts.2: SP, due to an incomplete trim change after gear extension, allowed downwind altitude to leave the 150 feet band. The deviation reached approximately 240 feet before SP recognized it on the altimeter and re-established the briefed altitude without assistance, well before the abeam position.
texts.3: SP established the briefed downwind altitude after the break and held it within 150 feet through the configuration changes. Trim was reset with each change, so the level flight path was maintained to the abeam position without correction.
texts.4: SP flew the whole downwind leg with altitude deviations that were barely readable on the altimeter, including through gear and flap extension. The aircraft was trimmed after each configuration change and required no altitude correction at any point.
texts.marginal: SP held downwind altitude inside the required standard, but the deviations reached the edge of the 150 feet band every time the configuration was changed. The tendency is to accept a descent during gear extension and then climb back. SP is expected to anticipate the trim change and hold altitude through the configuration change rather than correcting after it.

error_modes.label: Downwind airspeed and minimum speed compliance

texts.0: SP, due to inadequate monitoring of airspeed after the navigation recovery, allowed downwind speed to fall below the 120 KIAS minimum and to exceed the tolerance by more than 20 knots high earlier in the leg. Neither excursion was recognized from the airspeed indicator. The IP intervened on the throttle to restore the briefed downwind speed.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted cross-check while the landing checks were being run, allowed downwind airspeed to reach the plus 20 knots limit of the tolerance. The speed was reduced only after the IP called it, and the briefed value was regained late in the leg. The minimum of 120 KIAS was maintained throughout.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power reduction after the break, allowed downwind airspeed to leave the plus 10 knots band. The excess reached approximately 17 knots before SP cross-checked the airspeed indicator and set the briefed speed unaided, with the minimum of 120 KIAS never approached.
texts.3: SP placed the aircraft on downwind at the briefed speed with no value below the 120 KIAS minimum and no excess beyond 10 knots. The airspeed indicator was included in a continuous cross-check while the checks were run, so power adjustments were small and timely.
texts.4: SP set downwind airspeed at the briefed value immediately after the break and held it with excursions that were not measurable on the indicator. Speed remained clear of the 120 KIAS minimum at all times and no power correction was needed after the initial setting.
texts.marginal: SP kept downwind airspeed within the required standard, but the values sat at the top of the plus 10 knots band for most of the leg. The tendency is to carry surplus energy from the recovery into the pattern and bleed it off late. SP is expected to cross-check airspeed at fixed points on downwind and set the briefed value before the abeam position.

texts.0: SP, due to leaving power set for downwind while the descending turn was established, allowed base leg airspeed to exceed the tolerance by more than 20 knots. The excess was carried through the turn and left the aircraft high and fast at the roll-out point. The IP intervened on the throttle and controls to salvage the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power reduction entering base, allowed base leg airspeed to reach the plus 20 knots limit. The speed was reduced only after repeated calls from the IP, and the briefed value was not regained until the aircraft was almost on final.
texts.2: SP, due to an increased descent rate in the turn without a matching power change, allowed base leg airspeed to leave the plus 10 knots band. The excess reached approximately 16 knots before SP identified it and set the briefed speed unaided, with the correction complete before roll-out on final.
texts.3: SP established the briefed base leg speed at the start of the turn and held it within 10 knots to roll-out. Power and pitch were coordinated through the descending turn, so no speed excursion developed and the speed never fell below the briefed value.
texts.4: SP flew the base leg at the briefed speed with excursions that were not readable on the airspeed indicator. Power was set once at the start of the turn and the descending turn required no further speed correction.
texts.marginal: SP held base leg airspeed within the required standard, but the values sat at the upper edge of the plus 10 knots band throughout the turn. The tendency is to enter base with surplus speed and rely on the turn to bleed it off. SP is expected to set the briefed base leg power before starting the turn so the speed is stable from the beginning of the descent.

texts.0: SP, due to a roll-out point selected without reference to the planned final profile, arrived on final displaced beyond 200 feet high and later allowed the aircraft to sink more than 100 feet below the correct glidepath. Neither excursion was corrected as the runway was approached. The IP took control to re-establish the aircraft on the correct profile.
texts.1: SP, due to a descent started late on base, rolled out on final at the plus 200 feet deviation limit. The profile was corrected only after continuous verbal guidance from the IP, and the aircraft reached the correct glidepath late on final.
texts.2: SP, due to an under-planned roll-out point, arrived on final above the plus 100 feet band by approximately 160 feet. SP recognized the high profile on the visual references, adjusted power and pitch and re-established the correct glidepath before the aircraft reached the threshold area, without any assistance.
texts.3: SP rolled out on final on profile and held the glidepath within 100 feet high and 50 feet low to the threshold. The roll-out point was planned so that no large correction was required, and small power adjustments kept the aircraft on the correct descent path.
texts.4: SP arrived on final exactly on profile and flew the glidepath with deviations that were barely readable. The descent path was held with minimal power adjustments and the aircraft crossed the threshold area precisely on profile.
texts.marginal: SP kept final altitude within the required standard, but the profile sat near the plus 100 feet edge of the band on every pattern. The tendency is to plan the roll-out point slightly late and remain high to the threshold. SP is expected to start the base descent earlier so that the aircraft is on profile at roll-out rather than correcting down the final.

texts.0: SP, due to carrying surplus power into the roll-out and not re-setting it on final, exceeded the final airspeed tolerance by more than 15 knots. The excess speed was not reduced as the threshold was approached and the approach was no longer flyable to a landing. The IP intervened on the controls and throttle.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power reduction after roll-out on final, allowed final airspeed to reach the plus 15 knots limit. The speed was reduced only after repeated calls from the IP, and the briefed final speed was reached very close to the threshold.
texts.2: SP, due to a pitch change made before power was adjusted on final, allowed airspeed to leave the plus 10 knots band. The excess reached approximately 13 knots before SP cross-checked the airspeed indicator, set the briefed value unaided and had the speed stable well before the threshold.
texts.3: SP set the briefed final airspeed at roll-out and held it within 10 knots to the threshold, with no value below the briefed speed. Power adjustments were small and continuous, and the airspeed was stable through the last part of the approach.
texts.4: SP held final airspeed at the briefed value with excursions that were not measurable on the indicator. Power was trimmed once after roll-out and the approach required no further speed correction to the threshold.
texts.marginal: SP kept final airspeed within the required standard, but the values sat at the top of the plus 10 knots band for most of the final. The tendency is to fly the approach slightly fast and correct near the threshold. SP is expected to set the briefed final speed immediately at roll-out and hold it with small continuous power adjustments.

error_modes.label: AOA units on downwind, base and final (AOA pattern)
error_modes.source: specific:DOWN WIND - BASE - FINAL / AOA UNITS

texts.0: SP, due to flying the AOA pattern on airspeed alone without referring to the AOA indexer, allowed AOA to deviate beyond 3 units from the briefed value on base and final. The high AOA excursion was allowed to develop into the onset of buffet. The IP intervened on the controls to reduce the angle of attack.
texts.1: SP, due to an intermittent scan of the AOA indexer, allowed AOA to reach the 3 units deviation limit on the base leg. The correct AOA was re-established only after the IP called the indexer indication, and the excursion was repeated on final.
texts.2: SP, due to a pitch change made without a matching power adjustment, allowed AOA to leave the 1.5 units band on downwind. The deviation reached approximately 2.5 units before SP referred to the indexer and re-established the briefed AOA unaided before the turn to base.
texts.3: SP flew the AOA pattern with the indexer within 1.5 units of the briefed value on downwind, base and final. AOA was cross-checked continuously against airspeed and attitude, so pitch and power corrections were small and timely throughout.
texts.4: SP held the briefed AOA on downwind, base and final with deviations that were barely perceptible on the indexer. The correct angle of attack was maintained through both the configuration changes and the descending turn without any correction.
texts.marginal: SP kept AOA inside the required standard, but the indications sat at the high edge of the 1.5 units band through the base turn. The tendency is to add back pressure in the turn and then reduce it on final. SP is expected to keep the AOA indexer in the primary scan through the turn and to control angle of attack with power rather than pitch alone.

error_modes.label: Pattern entry, break zone, clearance, required checks and standardized reports

texts.0: SP, due to loss of situational awareness of the aircraft's position in the pattern after the navigation recovery, executed the break outside the break zone and without clearing the downwind. The landing checks were not completed and the standardized reports were not given. The IP intervened, took control and directed the pattern from the front cockpit.
texts.1: SP, due to degraded situational awareness on arrival at the field, entered the break zone without confirming ATC clearance and started the required checks late. The checks were completed and the standardized reports were passed only after the IP prompted for each of them, leaving the aircraft configured very late on downwind.
texts.2: SP, due to an attention split between the navigation recovery and the pattern entry, initially misidentified the break point and omitted one standardized report. SP recognized the error, cleared the downwind, repositioned into the break zone and passed the missing report and the required checks unprompted, before the turn to base.
texts.3: SP entered the pattern with ATC clearance, cleared the downwind and executed the break inside the break zone. The required checks were completed at the briefed points and within gear and flap limitations, and all standardized reports were passed correctly and on time.
texts.4: SP transitioned from the navigation recovery to the pattern without any loss of position awareness, breaking precisely in the break zone with clearance confirmed and the downwind cleared. Checks and standardized reports were completed exactly at the briefed points with no prompting and no interference with aircraft control.
texts.marginal: SP met the required standard for pattern entry, checks and reports, but the checks were consistently started at the late end of the acceptable window and one report needed a pause before transmission. The tendency is to begin the pattern tasks only after the aircraft is fully established rather than in parallel. SP is expected to build the pattern sequence into the recovery so that clearance, break zone identification, checks and reports are all completed on schedule.

error_modes.label: Base leg bank, final track and centerline alignment, go-around decision and stall avoidance

texts.0: SP, due to failure to call the go-around once the approach was no longer stable, continued an approach that was diverging from the final and was not aligned with the runway centerline inside 1/2 NM from the threshold. Bank on base exceeded 45 degrees during the attempt to correct back and stall characteristics began to appear. The IP took control, unloaded the aircraft and executed the go-around.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to state that the approach could not be continued, held a final track that converged on the centerline and reached alignment only very close to the threshold. Bank on base reached the 45 degrees limit during the correction, and the go-around was initiated only after the IP directed it, with a noticeable delay.
texts.2: SP, due to a roll-out point planned slightly inside the briefed one, initially converged on the final track and rolled out with the aircraft off the centerline. SP recognized the geometry early, corrected with bank well inside 45 degrees and was aligned with the runway centerline before 1/2 NM from the threshold, without prompting and without any approach to stall.
texts.3: SP planned the roll-out point as described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual, kept bank on base inside 45 degrees and neither deviated from nor converged on the final. The aircraft was aligned with the runway centerline well before 1/2 NM from the threshold and no stall characteristics were allowed to develop at any point.
texts.4: SP flew the base to final transition exactly on the planned roll-out point, arriving aligned on the runway centerline with no correction required. Bank remained comfortably inside the limit, the aircraft was flown clear of any approach to stall, and when a go-around was required it was initiated immediately and flown correctly without hesitation.
texts.marginal: SP met the required standard on final track and bank, but the roll-out consistently placed the aircraft slightly outside the centerline and alignment was achieved only just before 1/2 NM from the threshold. The tendency is to delay the assessment of whether the approach is still acceptable rather than stating it early. SP is expected to plan the roll-out point more precisely and to call a go-around promptly whenever the approach parameters are no longer being met.

error_modes.label: INITIAL POINT AIRSPEED, POWER SETTING AND RUNWAY ALIGNMENT

texts.0: SP, due to setting neither the 200 KIAS nor the 50 percent plus 1 percent per 1,000 feet MSL power called for at the initial point, arrived on initial fast and out of level flight. The aircraft was never aligned with the landing runway and pattern altitude was left by more than 300 feet before the break. The IP took control, re-established the initial and reset the power.
texts.1: SP, due to omitting the initial point power setting and chasing airspeed with the PCL, arrived on initial well above 200 KIAS and did not hold the alignment with the landing runway. Pattern altitude was allowed to reach the 300 feet limit and the offset from the runway extension was removed only after the IP called both the power and the altitude.
texts.2: SP, due to carrying cruise power instead of 50 percent plus 1 percent per 1,000 feet MSL, initially accelerated through 200 KIAS and drifted off the runway alignment. SP detected the trend on the crosscheck, reset power and pitch for level flight and regained pattern altitude within about 200 feet and the alignment before the break zone, without prompting.
texts.3: SP flew the initial point at 200 KIAS with power set at 50 percent plus 1 percent per 1,000 feet MSL and pitch as required for level flight. The aircraft was aligned with the landing runway as described in the local LAP and pattern altitude was held within 150 feet all the way to the break.
texts.4: SP arrived on initial exactly aligned with the landing runway, stabilized at 200 KIAS with the computed power set before the run-in. Pitch was trimmed for level flight and altitude and airspeed excursions were negligible up to the break.
texts.marginal: SP held 200 KIAS and pattern altitude inside limits on initial, but power was found by trial rather than computed, so airspeed was still settling as the break zone approached. Alignment with the landing runway was achieved late and the residual offset was always to the same side. SP is expected to set 50 percent plus 1 percent per 1,000 feet MSL early and to establish the runway alignment before the run-in rather than during it.

error_modes.label: BREAK POINT, BANK AND BACKPRESSURE VARIED WITH WIND AND TRAFFIC SPACING

texts.0: SP, due to flying a fixed break picture with no allowance for the wind, used the no-wind bank and backpressure and rolled out well off the desired downwind ground track. Bank differed from the value required by the conditions by more than 15 degrees during the attempted correction and the turn was not kept level, so pattern altitude was left by more than 300 feet. The IP took control to re-establish the downwind spacing and altitude.
texts.1: SP, due to not varying angle of bank and backpressure with the wind conditions, carried too little bank through the break and did not adjust the break point for traffic spacing. The correction reached the 15 degrees bank limit and the level decelerating turn lost altitude to the 300 feet limit, both being recovered only after the IP called for more bank and a check of the altitude.
texts.2: SP, due to using the briefed no-wind break picture, initially rolled in with less bank than the wind required and began to overshoot the planned downwind track. SP recognized it early, increased bank and backpressure to stay within about 10 degrees of the value required and held altitude inside 200 feet, arriving on inside downwind at 120 to 147 KIAS.
texts.3: SP adjusted the break point inside the break zone, between the approach end and 3,000 feet down the runway, for the wind and for traffic spacing, cleared in the direction of turn and rolled smoothly into 45 to 60 degrees of bank with power at approximately 10 percent. Bank and backpressure were varied with the wind so the level decelerating turn stayed within 10 degrees of the required bank and 150 feet of pattern altitude, and the aircraft slowed to 120 to 147 KIAS on inside downwind.
texts.4: SP selected the break point for the existing wind and for the traffic ahead, cleared the turn and flew the 180 degree level decelerating turn with bank and backpressure matched to the conditions. Altitude and bank excursions were negligible and the aircraft arrived on inside downwind on the planned ground track at 120 to 147 KIAS. When directed to break beyond the normal break point, SP maintained 200 KIAS until the break and lowered the gear at mid-field downwind.
texts.marginal: SP broke inside the break zone and stayed within the bank and altitude standards, but the same bank was used regardless of the wind, so the roll-out was repeatedly displaced from the planned downwind track and needed a correction. The level turn tended to sag toward the low end of the acceptable altitude band as airspeed decayed. SP is expected to vary angle of bank and backpressure with the wind conditions and to select the break point for spacing rather than by habit.

error_modes.label: TRIM DURING THE DECELERATING BREAK AND HANDS-OFF TRIM AFTER CONFIGURING

texts.0: SP, due to not trimming the control stick forces as airspeed decreased in the break and not trimming for zero control forces after the gear was lowered, flew the whole downwind holding a large out-of-trim force. The aircraft was never hands off, pattern altitude varied by more than 300 feet and airspeed was allowed to decay below the 120 KIAS minimum. The IP took control, trimmed the aircraft and re-established the downwind parameters.
texts.1: SP, due to leaving the trim set for break entry airspeed, carried a heavy stick force through the deceleration and did not trim to zero control forces after configuring. Pattern altitude reached the 300 feet limit and airspeed sat at the top of the band, 20 knots above the minimum, and trim was reset only after the IP called for it.
texts.2: SP, due to trimming only after each configuration change rather than continuously as airspeed decreased, initially held a noticeable stick force and let altitude wander by about 200 feet. SP recognized the out-of-trim state, trimmed for hands-off flight unprompted and had the aircraft stable at 120 KIAS minimum and on pattern altitude well before the perch point.
texts.3: SP trimmed control stick forces continuously as airspeed decreased in the break and trimmed for zero control forces, hands off, after lowering the gear. Pattern altitude was held within 150 feet and airspeed stayed within 10 knots above the 120 KIAS minimum with torque at approximately 30 to 35 percent.
texts.4: SP kept the aircraft in trim throughout the decelerating turn so that no stick force was carried at any airspeed, and the aircraft was hands off immediately after configuring. Altitude and airspeed excursions on downwind were negligible and the trim state required no further attention during the perch and final turn preparation.
texts.marginal: SP arrived at the perch trimmed and inside the downwind standards, but trim was applied in a few large inputs after each configuration change rather than as the airspeed decayed. The residual stick forces produced repeated altitude corrections at the edge of the acceptable band. SP is expected to trim continuously through the deceleration so that the aircraft is hands off from the moment the gear is down.

error_modes.label: DRIFT CORRECTION AND OFFSET OF THE DOWNWIND GROUND TRACK INTO THE WIND

texts.0: SP, due to flying the downwind heading with no drift correction and no offset of the inside downwind ground track into the wind, allowed the spacing to open far beyond the approximately half mile used in no-wind conditions. The geometry that resulted could not be flown within the normal ground track and, while chasing it, SP left pattern altitude by more than 300 feet. The IP took control and repositioned the aircraft on the downwind.
texts.1: SP, due to applying the same drift correction as used on initial instead of approximately twice that amount, let the ground track converge on the runway and the spacing close inside the planned distance. Pattern altitude reached the 300 feet limit during the attempt to rebuild the geometry, and the correct offset was flown only after the IP specified the drift correction to hold.
texts.2: SP, due to underestimating the effect of the wind on the final turn, initially did not offset the inside downwind ground track into the wind and the spacing began to close. SP identified the drift early, doubled the correction used on initial and re-established a ground track parallel to the runway, holding altitude within about 200 feet and reaching the perch at 120 KIAS minimum.
texts.3: SP applied drift correction of approximately twice that used on initial and offset the inside downwind ground track into the wind to account for the effect of the wind on the final turn. The ground track stayed parallel to the runway at about half a mile adjusted for the conditions, with pattern altitude held within 150 feet and airspeed within 10 knots above the minimum.
texts.4: SP established the drift correction immediately after roll-out from the break and flew a ground track exactly parallel to the runway at the spacing the wind required. The offset was set so that the final turn could be flown at the planned 30 degrees of bank, and altitude and airspeed excursions on downwind were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP maintained a parallel ground track and stayed within the downwind standards, but the drift correction was built up in small steps and the spacing settled at the wide end of the acceptable range. The offset for the effect of the wind on the final turn was applied only near the perch point. SP is expected to set approximately twice the correction used on initial at roll-out and to displace the ground track into the wind from the start of the downwind.

error_modes.label: PERCH POINT IDENTIFICATION AND DISPLACEMENT FOR WIND

texts.0: SP, due to starting the final turn without the touchdown point at approximately 45 degrees off the shoulder and without displacing the perch point into the wind, began the descending turn late with a strong headwind on final. The final was compressed well inside half a mile and the aircraft arrived more than 100 feet below the desired glidepath. The IP took control and executed a go-around.
texts.1: SP, due to using the no-wind perch picture with a headwind on final, did not begin the final turn earlier as the conditions required. The roll-out placed the aircraft at the low limit of the standard, 100 feet below the 3 to 4 degree glidepath at about half a mile, and the correction back to the glidepath was made only after the IP called the altitude.
texts.2: SP, due to judging the perch on distance rather than on the touchdown point being approximately 45 degrees off the shoulder, initially started the final turn slightly late. SP recognized the geometry, adjusted power and pitch and rolled out on the extended runway centerline at about half a mile within 75 feet of the desired glidepath, before any prompting.
texts.3: SP arrived at the perch point with the touchdown point approximately 45 degrees off the shoulder, properly configured and at 120 KIAS minimum, and displaced the perch point into the wind affecting the final turn. Roll-out was on the extended runway centerline between half and three quarters of a mile, with altitude within 100 feet above and 50 feet below the 3 to 4 degree glidepath.
texts.4: SP identified the perch point precisely from the 45 degree reference and corrected it for the wind on final without hesitation, beginning the final turn earlier into a headwind. The final turn produced a half to three quarter mile final on a 3 to 4 degree glidepath with negligible deviation and no correction required after roll-out.
texts.marginal: SP started each final turn from a perch that met the standard, but the point was consistently taken slightly past the 45 degree reference and the wind displacement was applied only once the drift became obvious. Roll-outs were repeatedly at the short end of the half to three quarter mile final with the glidepath just inside limits. SP is expected to displace the perch point into the wind and to begin the final turn earlier whenever a headwind is present on final.

error_modes.label: FINAL TURN ENTRY SEQUENCE FLAPS, POWER, PITCH, ROLL AND THE HALFWAY ALTITUDE CROSSCHECK

texts.0: SP, due to not using the flaps, power, pitch, roll prompt at the perch, rolled into the final turn before adjusting power and lowering the nose and did not counter the slight nose up produced as the flaps lowered. Halfway through the turn, perpendicular to the runway, the aircraft was far outside the 700 to 800 feet AGL expected in a 1,200 foot pattern and ended the turn more than 100 feet below the glidepath. The IP took control and flew a go-around.
texts.1: SP, due to omitting the power step of the flaps, power, pitch, roll sequence, entered the final turn nose high and allowed the aircraft to balloon as the flaps increased lift. The halfway crosscheck was well above the 700 to 800 feet AGL reference and the roll-out was at the 200 feet high limit on the glidepath, corrected only after the IP called for power and pitch.
texts.2: SP, due to applying the flaps, power, pitch, roll steps out of order, initially let the nose rise as the flaps lowered and the aircraft stayed high through the first part of the turn. SP used the crosscheck perpendicular to the runway, found the aircraft above the 700 to 800 feet AGL reference and corrected pitch and power to reach the roll-out within 100 feet of the desired glidepath.
texts.3: SP began the final turn with the flaps, power, pitch, roll prompt, anticipating the slight nose up as the flaps lowered, and made the gear down call when able. The composite crosscheck of the intended landing point, the rollout point and airspeed was maintained, and altitude halfway through the turn was approximately 700 to 800 feet AGL for the 1,200 foot pattern.
texts.4: SP flew the final turn entry as one smooth sequence, with power, pitch and bank set together and the flap induced pitch change absorbed without any altitude excursion. The halfway crosscheck matched the 700 to 800 feet AGL reference and the descent angle projected just short of the intended aim point, so the roll-out on final required no correction.
texts.marginal: SP used the correct entry prompt and met the standard, but power was normally set after the roll into bank, so the first part of every final turn was flown slightly high before being brought back. The halfway altitude crosscheck was made late and the aircraft met the reference only just inside limits. SP is expected to complete flaps, power, pitch, roll as a single action and to pick and visualize the rollout point before beginning the turn.

error_modes.label: BREAK-OUT FROM INSIDE DOWNWIND WHEN THE CRITERIA FOR CONTINUING ARE NOT MET

texts.0: SP, due to continuing a pattern whose spacing could not be maintained within the normal ground track, did not break out from inside downwind although the aircraft was not properly configured by the perch point and the traffic in the final turn was not in sight. The final turn was started anyway, the bank required went outside the standard and pattern altitude was left by more than 300 feet. The IP took control and broke the aircraft out of the pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to pressing on rather than accepting that the spacing had been lost, delayed the decision to break out from inside downwind. Downwind airspeed and altitude reached the limits of the standard while the spacing was worked, and the break-out was flown only after the IP directed it.
texts.2: SP, due to a late start on the configuration, approached the perch point without being properly configured. SP recognized that the criteria for continuing were not met, broke out from inside downwind using local procedures without prompting, and re-entered with airspeed within 10 knots of the minimum and altitude within 150 feet.
texts.3: SP checked the pattern against the published break-out criteria and broke out from inside downwind, pattern status permitting, when the aircraft was not properly configured by the perch point and when spacing could not be maintained within the normal ground track. Downwind airspeed stayed within 10 knots above the minimum and altitude within 150 feet throughout.
texts.4: SP assessed the pattern continuously against the break-out criteria and decided early, always before the perch point, so the break-out was flown as a planned manoeuvre with negligible altitude and airspeed excursions. Traffic in the final turn, straight-in aircraft inside 2 miles, spacing and configuration were all covered by the decision and stated clearly on the intercom.
texts.marginal: SP did break out when the criteria required it and stayed within the downwind standards, but the decision came at the perch point after an attempt to salvage the spacing. Configuration on those patterns was completed at the late end of the acceptable window. SP is expected to check the break-out criteria abeam the tower and to decide early rather than at the last acceptable moment.

error_modes.label: FORMATION RECOVERY BREAK INTERVAL AND DOWNWIND POSITION AS NUMBER 2
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, as Number 2, due to starting the turn less than the minimum of 5 seconds after Number 1's Break, arrived on downwind with no usable spacing and inside Number 1's ground track. SP then followed a poorly flown pattern instead of going around, and downwind altitude and airspeed were left outside the standard by more than 300 feet and 20 knots. The IP took control and took the aircraft out of the pattern.
texts.1: SP, as Number 2, due to breaking early without taking the full 5 second interval, closed the downwind spacing and had to fly inside Number 1's ground track. Downwind altitude and airspeed reached the limits of the standard while the spacing was rebuilt, and the go-around was flown only after the IP directed it.
texts.2: SP, as Number 2, due to judging the interval by feel rather than taking the minimum of 5 seconds, initially turned early and drifted inside Number 1's downwind ground track. SP recognized the closure, moved the ground track to the outside as required and re-established the spacing, with airspeed corrected inside 10 knots and altitude inside 150 feet before the perch point.
texts.3: SP, as Number 2, waited a minimum of 5 seconds after Number 1's Break before starting the turn and flew the downwind slightly outside Number 1's ground track. The rest was flown as a normal contact pattern with the same perch point, holding downwind airspeed within 10 knots above the minimum and altitude within 150 feet.
texts.4: SP, as Number 2, took the interval precisely, rolled out with correct spacing and held a downwind ground track just outside Number 1's, with negligible altitude and airspeed excursions. When Number 1's pattern developed poorly, SP did not follow it but flew a go-around immediately and re-entered as briefed.
texts.marginal: SP, as Number 2, met the interval and the downwind standards, but the turn was consistently started at the earliest acceptable moment and the ground track was only just outside Number 1's. Spacing was then held with power changes on downwind rather than being set by the initial interval. SP is expected to take the full interval after Number 1's Break and to set the downwind offset at roll-out so that the perch point can be flown normally.
